title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Hyperscale Data switches to AI in Cass Co as communities weigh power, water and tax impacts.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.

Tonight we're zeroing in on Hyperscale Data's shift in Cass County from Bitcoin mining to AI operations, and how it fits into the bigger statewide tug-of-war over who pays for the power and water these facilities demand.
So Graham, walk me through what happened today with this announcement.

Hyperscale Data is shutting down all its Bitcoin miners at the Michigan site effective September 1. They're moving under a master services agreement that could bring in 1.2 billion dollars, with options that might push the total to 3 billion. The AI work would use up to 20 percent of the facility's 340 megawatt capacity.
Why does switching from mining to AI matter for the rest of us? Aren't both power hogs?

They are, but AI workloads tend to run more consistently and at higher intensity than crypto mining, which can ramp up and down. That steady draw puts real pressure on the grid, especially when you add cooling needs that pull water from local supplies.
And Cass County is in southwest Michigan, right? How does this connect to the fights we're seeing in Ionia, Decatur, or even Detroit?

Exactly. The same concerns about electricity rates, groundwater, and land use are popping up everywhere a project gets proposed. Residents 30 miles away from Ionia are already asking questions because new facilities could push up bills and strain aquifers.
What's the history here? Have these projects been moving fast, or has there been pushback building for a while?

It's been building. Places like Ypsilanti debated a year-long pause just yesterday, Decatur residents clashed over taxes, noise, and grid impacts, and Detroit groups are calling for a freeze while rules get written. The pattern is communities trying to get ahead of proposals instead of reacting after plans are filed.
Who are the main players in Cass County and beyond?

On one side you have the company, Hyperscale Data, promising big revenue and possible expansion. On the other, local residents, township boards, and utilities like Consumers Energy that have to upgrade infrastructure. Then there are lawmakers weighing in on taxes and local control.
How do these projects typically affect electric bills for regular folks?

The upgrades needed to serve a 340 megawatt user don't come cheap. Utilities spread those costs across all ratepayers, so even if the data center pays its share, households often see increases. That's why Mike Rogers called yesterday for a statewide pause until utilities prove they can handle the load without hikes.
And water? I keep hearing about cooling systems.

Data centers use millions of gallons for evaporative cooling. In areas already watching groundwater levels, that adds up fast. St. Clair County is holding a workshop soon specifically on noise, air, and water risks for that reason.
What about farmland and small towns? Does the land use change the character of these places?

It can. A large campus takes acres that might have been farming or open space. Supporters point to jobs and tax revenue, but opponents worry about higher property taxes for neighbors and the loss of rural feel. Decatur's debate yesterday showed both sides clearly.
So what happens next with this Cass County site?

The company has room to expand within that 20 percent capacity slice. If AI demand keeps growing, we could see more phases. Meanwhile, other townships are watching to see if they need stricter zoning before similar proposals land.
And how does this fit with the tax break debate?

Senator Runestad pushed yesterday to end sales-tax exemptions for new data centers. That could mean more revenue for the state but also higher costs passed along if projects slow down or get more expensive to build.
Rep. James is arguing for local control instead. What's the tension there?

He wants cities and townships to set their own rules. Some see that as protecting community voices; others note his past federal votes leaned toward limiting local authority. The shift could change how approvals happen across Michigan.
Bottom line for listeners 30 or 60 miles away from Cass County?
The same dynamics are playing out statewide. Power demand is rising, water is finite, and towns are scrambling to write rules before the next proposal arrives.
Thanks for laying that out. Let's move to some quick hits from around the state.
Starting with Ionia. Residents there got their first look today at potential data center power and water risks during a proactive public meeting, even though no formal proposals have arrived yet.
And 30 miles away people are paying attention because rates and groundwater could be affected. Smart move to get ahead of it.
Next, St. Clair County. Locals will hear about health risks like noise, air, and water impacts at an upcoming workshop. The discussion could shape zoning fights in southeast Michigan.
Power grid strain and drinking water supplies are the big worries if projects advance there.
Rep. James is out today pushing local control over data center rules. He says cities and townships should decide for themselves.
That could reshape approvals statewide depending on how it lands with other lawmakers.

Yesterday Consumers Energy started work on Cherry Street to bolster the grid for rising loads from data centers and other big users. West Michigan customers may see more construction and rate impacts down the road.
Tied directly to the surging demand we're talking about.
Senator Runestad also moved yesterday to repeal sales-tax breaks for new data centers. The idea is to shift more costs onto residents and local governments instead of giving exemptions.
Lawmakers will have to balance that revenue against the job and investment arguments.
In Decatur yesterday, residents clashed over a proposed campus, focusing on property taxes, noise, and the power grid. Supporters highlight jobs; neighbors fear higher utility bills and water use.
Sounds like a test case for other small towns facing similar proposals.
Detroit residents are facing blackout risk concerns as groups demand a freeze on new data centers while the city writes rules on power and water use.
A moratorium would give time to assess impacts on ratepayers and neighborhoods.
Mike Rogers called yesterday for a statewide pause on new construction until utilities can prove they can handle the added thousands of megawatts without hiking bills.
Voters across parties have voiced concern over who ultimately pays for the upgrades.
And in Ypsilanti yesterday, city leaders weighed a year-long halt on standalone data center proposals. Residents worry about electricity rates and water supply.
That would buy time to craft permanent zoning rules.
Let's look ahead to what's coming up for listeners who want to get involved.
St. Clair County has that public workshop on health and environmental risks scheduled soon. It's a chance for locals to weigh in before any projects move forward.
Ionia's meeting today gave residents an early seat at the table. Other townships are likely watching how that went.
And keep an eye on council sessions in places like Ypsilanti if they follow up on the pause discussion.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.
Good night, everyone.

episode_title: Cass County Pivot: Hyperscale Data Trades Bitcoin for AI Amid Growing Local Pushback
